title: Fill in: He is good ___ mathematics.
statement: Fill in the blank: "He is good ___ mathematics."
explanation: The fixed expression is **good at** a subject or skill.

title: Fill in: The train arrived ___ time; it was neither early nor late.
statement: Fill in the blank: "The train arrived ___ time; it was neither early nor late."
explanation: **On time** means punctually. *In time* means early enough (before it was too late).

title: Fill in: She prefers tea ___ coffee.
statement: Fill in the blank: "She prefers tea ___ coffee."
explanation: **Prefer** takes *to*: prefer X **to** Y. *Than* is used with *rather* (I would rather have tea than coffee).

title: Fill in: I have lived in Pune ___ ten years.
statement: Fill in the blank: "I have lived in Pune ___ ten years."
explanation: Use **for** with a duration (ten years) and *since* with a starting point (2015).

title: Fill in: Neither of the answers ___ correct.
statement: Fill in the blank: "Neither of the answers ___ correct."
explanation: **Neither** (of …) is singular in formal English, so it takes **is**.

title: Fill in: The news ___ very encouraging.
statement: Fill in the blank: "The news ___ very encouraging."
explanation: **News** is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb, despite ending in *s*.

title: Fill in: He ___ to the gym every morning.
statement: Fill in the blank: "He ___ to the gym every morning."
explanation: A habitual action in the present with a third-person singular subject: **goes**.

title: Fill in: She is ___ honest woman.
statement: Fill in the blank: "She is ___ honest woman."
explanation: The *h* in *honest* is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound: **an** honest woman.

title: Fill in: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
statement: Fill in the blank: "Mathematics ___ my favourite subject."
explanation: Names of subjects ending in *-ics* (mathematics, physics, economics) take a **singular** verb.

title: Fill in: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer.
statement: Fill in the blank: "If I ___ you, I would accept the offer."
explanation: Imaginary (unreal) conditions use the subjunctive **were** for every subject: *If I were you…*

title: Fill in: The children were tired, so they went ___ bed early.
statement: Fill in the blank: "The children were tired, so they went ___ bed early."
explanation: The idiom is **go to bed** — no article. *Go to the bed* means walking over to the piece of furniture.

title: Fill in: He has been absent ___ Monday.
statement: Fill in the blank: "He has been absent ___ Monday."
explanation: **Since** introduces a point in time (Monday) with the present perfect.

title: Fill in: She is the ___ student in the class.
statement: Fill in the blank: "She is the ___ student in the class."
explanation: Comparing one person with the whole class needs the superlative **tallest**. *More taller* is a double comparative.

title: Fill in: We discussed ___ the problem for an hour.
statement: Fill in the blank: "We discussed ___ the problem for an hour."
explanation: **Discuss** is transitive: you *discuss a problem*, not *discuss about* it.

title: Fill in: My brother and I ___ going to the market.
statement: Fill in the blank: "My brother and I ___ going to the market."
explanation: Two subjects joined by *and* form a plural subject: **are**.

title: Fill in: There ___ a lot of people at the concert.
statement: Fill in the blank: "There ___ a lot of people at the concert."
explanation: With *a lot of* the verb agrees with the noun that follows: *people* is plural, so **were**.

title: Correct sentence: number of
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The number of applicants have increased this year.
The numbers of applicants has increased this year.
The number of applicant has increased this year.
The number of applicants has increased this year.
explanation: **The number of** + plural noun takes a **singular** verb (the subject is *number*). Compare *A number of applicants **have** applied*, which is plural.

title: Correct sentence: hardly when
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Hardly had I reach the station when the train left.
Hardly had I reached the station than the train left.
Hardly I had reached the station when the train left.
Hardly had I reached the station when the train left.
explanation: **Hardly … when** (not *than*). Starting with *Hardly* inverts the subject and auxiliary: *had I reached*.

title: Correct sentence: no sooner
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: No sooner did he arrived than the meeting began.
No sooner did he arrive than the meeting began.
No sooner did he arrive when the meeting began.
No sooner he arrived than the meeting began.
explanation: **No sooner … than** (not *when*), with inversion: *did he arrive* (base form after *did*).

title: Correct sentence: each has his
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Each of the boys has submitted his assignment.
Each of the boys have submitted his assignment.
Each of the boys have submitted their assignments.
Each of the boy has submitted his assignment.
explanation: **Each** is singular, so the verb is **has** and the noun after *of* stays plural (*the boys*).

title: Correct sentence: furniture
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The furniture in the office is new.
The furnitures in the office are new.
The furniture in the office are new.
The furnitures in the office is new.
explanation: **Furniture** is uncountable: no plural *-s*, and it takes a singular verb (*is*).

title: Correct sentence: look forward
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: I look forward to met you.
I look forward to meet you.
I look forward to meeting you.
I look forward for meeting you.
explanation: In **look forward to**, *to* is a preposition, so it is followed by the *-ing* form: *to meeting*.

title: Correct sentence: one of those
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: He is one of those people who never gives up.
He is one of those people who never give up.
He is one of those person who never give up.
He is one of that people who never give up.
explanation: In *one of those people who…*, the relative pronoun **who** refers to *people* (plural), so the verb is **give**.

title: Correct sentence: scarcely when
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Scarcely had we started than it began to rain.
Scarcely we had started when it began to rain.
Scarcely had we started when it began to rain.
Scarcely had we start when it began to rain.
explanation: **Scarcely … when**, with inversion (*had we started*), like *hardly … when*.

title: Correct sentence: police have
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The police have arrest the thief.
The police have arrested the thief.
The police has arrested the thief.
The polices have arrested the thief.
explanation: **Police** is a plural noun in English: *the police **have***. It never takes *-s*.

title: Spot the error: He did not knew the answer to the last question.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) He did not knew / (B) the answer to / (C) the last question. / (D) No error
explanation: After *did* (or *did not*) use the base form: *did not **know***.

title: Spot the error: The committee have submitted its report.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) The committee / (B) have submitted / (C) its report. / (D) No error
explanation: *Its report* treats the committee as a single unit, so the verb must be singular too: *has submitted*.

title: Spot the error: Unless you do not work hard, you will not pass the exam.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) Unless you do not work hard, / (B) you will not / (C) pass the exam. / (D) No error
options: (A) Unless you do not work hard,
explanation: **Unless** already means *if not*; adding *do not* makes a double negative. Correct: *Unless you work hard…*

title: Spot the error: Despite of the rain, the match continued as planned.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) Despite of the rain, / (B) the match / (C) continued as planned. / (D) No error
explanation: **Despite** is never followed by *of*. Use *despite the rain* or *in spite of the rain*.

title: Spot the error: He has returned from Delhi yesterday.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) He has returned / (B) from Delhi / (C) yesterday. / (D) No error
explanation: A finished past time (*yesterday*) needs the simple past: *He **returned** from Delhi yesterday*. The present perfect can't take a past time marker.

title: Spot the error: Neither Ravi nor his friends was present at the meeting.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) Neither Ravi / (B) nor his friends / (C) was present at the meeting. / (D) No error
explanation: With *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject — *his friends* (plural) → *were present*.

title: Correct sentence: between you and me
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Among you and me, the plan won't work.
Between you and I, the plan won't work.
Between you and me, the plan won't work.
Between you and myself, the plan won't work.
explanation: **Between** is a preposition, so it takes object pronouns: *between you and **me***. *Among* is for more than two.

title: Correct sentence: more of two
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: She is the more intelligent of the two sisters.
She is more intelligent of the two sisters.
She is the most intelligent of the two sisters.
She is the intelligenter of the two sisters.
explanation: Comparing **two** uses the comparative with *the*: *the more intelligent of the two*. The superlative is for three or more.

title: Correct sentence: ten kilometres
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Ten kilometre is a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometres are long distance to walk.
explanation: An amount of distance, money or time treated as one quantity takes a **singular** verb: *Ten kilometres **is** a long distance*.

title: Fill in: He insisted ___ paying the bill.
statement: Fill in the blank: "He insisted ___ paying the bill."
explanation: **Insist** takes *on* + *-ing*: *insisted on paying*.

title: Spot the error: Not only the students but also the teacher were invited to the event.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) Not only the students / (B) but also the teacher / (C) were invited to the event. / (D) No error
explanation: With *not only … but also*, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject — *the teacher* (singular) → *was invited*.

title: Correct sentence: had i known
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Had I knew about the delay, I would take another route.
Had I known about the delay, I would have taken another route.
If I would have known about the delay, I would have taken another route.
If I had known about the delay, I would take another route.
explanation: A past unreal condition uses the past perfect in the *if*-clause (or the inverted *Had I known*) and *would have* + past participle in the result. *If I would have known* is incorrect.

title: Correct sentence: reason is that
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The reason why he failed is because he did not prepare.
The reason he failed is because he did not prepare.
The reason he failed is that he did not prepare.
The reason he failed was because of he did not prepare.
explanation: **The reason … is that** — *because* repeats the idea of *reason*, so *the reason is because* is redundant.

title: Spot the error: Being a rainy day, we decided to stay indoors.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) Being a rainy day, / (B) we decided / (C) to stay indoors. / (D) No error
explanation: A dangling participle: *Being a rainy day* seems to describe *we*. Correct: *It being a rainy day, we decided…* or *As it was a rainy day…*

title: Correct sentence: not until
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Not until the results announced did she relax.
Not until the results were announced did she relax.
Not until the results were announced she relaxed.
Not until were the results announced did she relax.
explanation: A sentence starting with **Not until** inverts the *main* clause (*did she relax*); the *until*-clause keeps normal order.

title: Spot the error: The cost of these new phones are rising every year.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) The cost of / (B) these new phones / (C) are rising every year. / (D) No error
explanation: The subject is **cost** (singular), not *phones*: *The cost … **is** rising*.

title: Correct sentence: hardly anyone
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Hardly no one attended the lecture.
Hardly any one did not attended the lecture.
Hardly anyone didn't attend the lecture.
explanation: **Hardly** is already negative, so it can't be combined with *no one* or *didn't* (double negative).

title: Spot the error: He is so tired that he cannot hardly walk.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) He is so tired / (B) that he / (C) cannot hardly walk. / (D) No error
explanation: *Cannot hardly* is a double negative. Correct: *he can hardly walk*.

title: Correct sentence: whom invite
statement: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Who did you invited to the party?
Whom did you invite to the party?
Whom did you invited to the party?
Whom you did invite to the party?
explanation: The pronoun is the object of *invite*, so formal English uses **whom**; after *did*, the verb is the base form (*invite*), and the question needs inversion (*did you*).

title: Spot the error: The manager, along with his assistants, are attending the conference today.
statement:
The sentence below is split into parts. Which part contains an error? (Choose *No error* if it is correct.)

(A) The manager, along with his assistants, / (B) are attending / (C) the conference today. / (D) No error
options: (A) The manager, along with his assistants,
explanation: Phrases like *along with*, *as well as* and *together with* don't change the subject: *The manager … **is** attending*.
